p.seg: Kǒngzǐ Jí Yǔ
Compiled by Xuē Jù of the Sòng dynasty.
Jù's courtesy name was Shūróng,
a native of Yǒngjiā.
He served as the Ever-Normal Granary Intendant of Eastern Zhè.
Lín Déyáng's "Collection from Mount Jì" contains a preface to the Collected Works of the Two Mr. Xuē, saying:
"The Xuē family's learning has spanned three hundred years.
Lord Yùchéng studied under Yáng Jìngzhòng of Lake Cí,
discarding the flowery and adhering to the substantial,
like the remaining strands from the school of the Chéng brothers.
When false learning flourished and was prohibited,
he single-handedly defended the Way,
He authored *Zhuó Yī Luò Yuán Liú*,
each forming a genealogy.
Furthermore, he imparted the methods of bow-making and metal-casting to his son, Gōng Shūróng,
whose ambitions were grand and whose strength was resolute,
bearing the burden of a thousand years.
Lamenting the distance from the sages and the obscurity of their words,
he compiled the *Kǒngzǐ Jí Yǔ* in twenty *juǎn* (scrolls/chapters),
which is this very book.
This edition only divides it into twenty sections,
comprising merely three *juǎn*.
Perhaps, in older times, one section was considered one *juǎn*,
which later generations combined.
The listed books number more than thirty.

Its general principles state that the four complete books, *Zēngzǐ*, *Dà Dài Lǐ*, *Kǒng Cóngzǐ*, and *Kǒngzǐ Jiā Yǔ*, as well as *Zuǒ Shì*, *Zhuāngzǐ*, *Xúnzǐ*, and *Lièzǐ*, are generally not adopted,
only those found in other ancient books are selected.
However, the *Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā* is listed in the official history,
not deviating from *Kǒng Cóng Jiā Yǔ*.
Moreover, it states that it will not include *Dà Dài Lǐ Jì*,
yet Yán Shūzǐ chapter twelve cites one passage from it,
contradicting its own rules.
Furthermore, it cites the *Shuōwén* on how millet can be used to make wine,
that grain enters the water,
that "one piercing through three" signifies a king,
and that "pushing one to combine with ten" signifies a *shì* (scholar), etc.,
combining several entries into one,
whose meanings are unrelated,
which is especially incoherent.
As for the *Hán Fēizǐ*, the chapters *Shuō Lín Xià*, *Nèi Chǔ Shuō Shàng*, *Nèi Chǔ Shuō Xià*, *Wài Chǔ Shuō Zuǒ Shàng*, *Wài Chǔ Shuō Yòu Xià*, *Nán Yī*, and *Nán Sān*,
There were twenty or so items that could be selected,
but this book only cites three.
For example, in the *Huáinánzǐ*, the chapters "Dào Yīng Xùn," "Zhǔ Shù Xùn," "Xià Qí Sú Xùn," "Xiū Wù Xùn," "Tài Sú Xùn," and "Yào Lüè,"
there are no fewer than ten items that could be selected,
but this only cites three as well.
Thus, the remaining omissions
can be generally understood.
Furthermore, Wén Xiángfèng's *Yún Mèng Yào Xī Tán*
extracts one item about "Wǔ Yǒu,"
citing *Sōushén Jì* while concealing its source,
and also mistakenly writes "Wǔ Yǒu" as "Wǔ Qiú."
Therefore, its mixed nature and errors
are also unavoidable.
However, it records many ancient Qin and Hàn books,
fragments and incomplete sentences,
which may be preserved only through this.
Therefore, those who study ancient texts cannot disregard it.
Preface
The *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ*
was compiled by Sūn Xīngyǎn of Yánghú, styled Bóyuān, who served as an observation commissioner.
Confucius elucidated the way of a hundred kings to instruct posterity.
Beyond the Six Classics,
the subtle words and profound meanings recorded in biographies and various schools of thought
are sufficient to aid the Classics and promote Confucian ideals,
and they often appear.
Among those compiled into books,
Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng dynasty's *Kǒngzǐ Zhèngyán* in twenty volumes and Wáng Bó's *Cì Lúnyǔ* in ten volumes
have not survived to the present day.
Extant are Yáng Jiǎn's 楊簡 *Xiānsheng Dàxùn* 《先聖大訓》 in ten volumes, Xuē Jù's 薛據 *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* 《孔子集語》 in two volumes, and Pān Shìdá's 潘士達 *Lúnyǔ Wàipiān* 《論語外篇》 in twenty volumes.
Xuē's 薛 book is the most prominent,
but it inevitably has omissions and oversights.
Recently, Cáo Tíngdòng 曹廷棟
also compiled *Kǒngzǐ Yìyǔ* 《孔子逸語》 in ten volumes,
but his research was inaccurate and lacked verification,
so it is not worth discussing.
In the *xīnwèi* 辛未 year of the Jiāqìng 嘉慶 era
(1811), the *guānchá* 觀察 [official title, lit. "observer," often a provincial surveillance commissioner] retired from office due to illness.
Lamenting the deficiencies and omissions in Confucian texts,
he extensively searched through various books,
comprehensively verifying and comparing different versions.
He increased Xuē's 薛 book by six or seven times
but still named it *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* 《孔子集語》;
this shows the principles behind his work.
The general rules for his compilation are as follows:

The *Yì Shíyì* 《易十翼》 (Ten Wings Commentary on the Book of Changes), *Lǐ Xiǎo Dàijì* 《禮小戴記》 (Record of Rituals by Dài the Younger), *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* 《春秋左氏傳》 (Zuo Tradition Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals), *Xiàojīng* 《孝經》 (Classic of Filial Piety), *Lúnyǔ* 《論語》 (Analects), and *Mèngzǐ* 《孟子》 (Mencius)
are universally recited and studied,
so they are not included.
The *Jiāyǔ* 《家語》 (School Sayings of Confucius) and *Kǒng Cóngzǐ* 《孔叢子》 (Master Kong's Family Sayings)
are complete books that circulate independently,
so they are not included.
The "Kongzi Shijia" 孔子世家 (Hereditary House of Confucius) and "Dizi Zhuan" 弟子傳 (Biographies of Disciples) in the *Shǐjì* 《史記》 (Records of the Grand Historian)
are easy to find, so they are also not included.
As for the remaining commentaries on the Classics, apocryphal texts, various histories, and philosophical works,
as well as anthologies from the Tang and Song dynasties,
both lengthy passages and single sentences are fully recorded,
without selection or omission.
All clearly state the source of the passages, volume by volume.
In cases where there were suspected omissions or incomplete sentences,
appropriate annotations were added.
Some matters are mutually referenced in different places,
even appearing five or six times.
Strengths and weaknesses, merits and shortcomings,
can be mutually verified and understood.
After more than a year,
the initial draft was completed.
Two years later,
it was entrusted to his friend Yūchéng Yán Kějūn of Wūchéng,
who, roughly imitating the style of the *Shuō Yuàn* (Garden of Stories),
organized and oversaw it.
Re-examining many books,
correcting erroneous characters,
rearranging the order,
adding to what was missing,
resulted in fourteen chapters:
"Exhortation to Learning" (Quàn Xué) being the first,
"The Foundation of Filial Piety" (Xiào Běn) the second,
"The Five Natures" (Wǔ Xìng) the third,
"The Six Arts" (Liù Yì) the fourth,
"The Virtue of the Ruler" (Zhǔ Dé) the fifth,
"The Art of the Minister" (Chén Shù) the sixth,
"The Way of Association" (Jiāo Dào) the seventh,
"On People" (Lùn Rén) the eighth,
"On Governance" (Lùn Zhèng) the ninth,
"Natural History" (Bówù) the tenth,
Chapter Eleven: Records of Affairs,
Chapter Twelve: Miscellaneous Matters,
Chapter Thirteen: Extant Prophecies,
Chapter Fourteen: Allegories.
Each chapter is a scroll;
the scrolls of the Six Arts, Records of Affairs, and Allegories are large,
and are divided into upper and lower sections,
making seventeen scrolls out of fourteen chapters.
Chapters such as "Exhortation to Learning"
are closely related to the main text.
The Extant Prophecies are not pure,
the Allegories are likely based on conjecture.
It was then printed in Jīnlíng
and made public to later generations.
-- Preface by Yán Kějūn.
Memorial
Sūn Xīngyǎn, your subject, Commissioner of Grain Transport for Shāndōng, kowtows and respectfully submits this memorial, saying,
your subject's completed *Kǒngzǐ Jíyǔ* (Collected Sayings of Confucius) in fourteen chapters,
I respectfully present it in this memorial for your consideration.
Humbly, Huáng Zhuān transmitted the Dao,
and the Vermillion Book was prepared with the ceremony of facing north;
the River Chart and Luo River Writing emerged,
and Yuánhù had the custom of an eastern tour.
To reconcile diverse opinions, one awaits the ultimate sage,
and examining the ancients is how one aligns with Heaven.
I respectfully reflect that our Emperor elegantly praises the classics,
and venerates the Sage in the Imperial Academy.
As vast as Heaven,
Yáo's essence is hard to name;
like the sun diligently shining,
Yǔ thought of listening to good advice.
What is gathered from the grass and firewood is indispensable;
moreover, instructions and guidance have clear evidence.
In the past, Confucius,
Attached to the Duke of Qūelǐ,
Recounting the ancestral virtue of the Sage's school.
Respectfully presented for Your Majesty's perusal,
May it serve as an aid at your side,
Widely disseminated throughout the Confucian community,
And humbly compared to the texts found in the wall.
Your subject is overcome with trepidation and awe,
Gazing at the heavens and longing for the imperial palace,
Leaping with joy and elation.
Respectfully presented through Yǎnshèng Gōng, your subject Qìngróng,
Submitting this memorial to Your Majesty for your kind attention.

Exhortation to Learning 1
*Shàngshū Dàzhuàn · Lüèshuō* (Commentary on the Book of Documents - Abridged Explanation) Confucius said:
“A *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) cannot but learn;
when seeing others, one cannot but be presentable.
Without being presentable, there is no proper appearance;
without proper appearance, there is no respect;
without respect, there are no rites;
without rites, one cannot be established.
That which shines from afar
is being presentable;
that which becomes brighter upon closer inspection
is learning.
It is like a ditch;
collected floodwaters gather there,
and rushes and reeds grow.
When viewed from above,
who would know that it is not spring water!"
*Dà Dài Lǐ · Quàn Xué* (The Great Dai Ritual - Exhortation to Learning) Confucius said:
"How uncultivated!
A *jūnzǐ* cannot but learn;
when seeing others, one cannot but be adorned.
Without adornment, there is no proper appearance;
without proper appearance, there is no respect;
without respect, there are no rites;
without rites, one cannot be established.
That which shines from afar
is adornment;
That which, being near, becomes even brighter,
is learning.
It is like a dirty and foul place
where accumulated rainwater gathers,
and rushes and cattails grow.
Viewing it from above,
who would know that it is not a spring!"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Lǐ,
a gentleman must not fail to learn,
and when seeing people, must not fail to adorn himself.
If he does not adorn himself, he will have no root;
if he has no root, he will lose principle;
if he loses principle, he will be disloyal;
if he is disloyal, he will lose ritual propriety;
if he loses ritual propriety, he will not be able to stand.
That which, being distant, has light,
is adornment;
that which, being near, becomes even brighter,
is learning.
It is like a dirty pond
where accumulated rainwater flows,
and *jiān* rushes and cattails grow.
Viewing it from above,
one knows that it is not a spring."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A gentleman has three worries:
not knowing,
Can one be without worry?
Knowing but not learning,
Can one be without worry?
Learning but not practicing,
Can one be without worry?"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* Six. Zǐ Yuē (Confucius said):
"To not learn but to like thinking,
though one knows, it will not be extensive;
to learn but be negligent in self-cultivation,
though one learns, one will not be respected;
to not establish oneself with sincerity,
though one stands, it will not be for long;
if sincerity is not manifested but one likes to speak,
though one speaks, it will not be believed.
A beautiful talent,
but not hearing the Dào of the Jūnzǐ.
Concealing small things to harm great things,
calamity will surely befall oneself."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* Six. Kǒngzǐ said:
"Those with whom one can talk all day without weariness,
it is only through learning!
Their physical body is not worth looking at,
their courage and strength are not worth fearing,
their clan name is not worth mentioning,
their ancestors are not worth talking about,
but they can be heard in all directions and known among the lords,
it is only through learning!"
*Shuō Yuàn · Jiàn Běn*. Kǒngzǐ said:
"That which allows one to spend the entire day with others without fatigue,
is perhaps only learning!
One's physical appearance is not worth admiring,
one's courage and strength are not worth fearing,
one's ancestors are not worth praising,
one's clan name is not worth mentioning,
yet one can open up the four quarters and become well-known among the various lords;
it is perhaps only learning!"
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, chapter eight. Kǒngzǐ was relaxing in his leisure when
Zǐgòng adjusted his clothes and stepped forward, saying:
"Your disciple has served you, Master, for many years.
My talent is exhausted and my wisdom fatigued.
I exert myself in learning,
but I dare not advance further.
I beg for a rest."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Where do you, Cì, wish to rest?" He said:
"I wish to rest from serving a ruler."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'From early morning until late at night, without negligence,
to serve one person.'
To do it like this
is not easy.
How can you rest!" He said:
"I wish to rest from serving my parents."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
“A filial son is never lacking,
And will forever be blessed with your kind.”
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?" Zì Gòng said,
"Cì wishes to find rest in serving his brothers."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Wife and children in good accord,
Like playing the sè and qín.
When brothers are united,
They are harmonious, happy, and content.'
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?" Zì Gòng said,
"Cì wishes to find rest in farming."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'By day, you gather thatch;
By night, you twist rope.
Quickly you climb the roof,
And then you begin to sow all the grains.'
To achieve this state is
not easy.
How can one find rest?"
Zǐ Gòng said,
"Does the junzi ever rest?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Only when the coffin is closed does the sowing cease,
unaware that time easily passes.
This is what is called the gentleman's rest."
*Xúnzǐ · Dàlüè*: Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Sì is weary of learning
and wishes to cease serving the ruler."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Be gentle and respectful morning and night,
perform your duties with diligence.'
Serving a ruler is difficult,
how can serving a ruler be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to cease serving his parents."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'A filial son is never deficient,
may you always receive blessings.'
Serving parents is difficult,
how can serving parents be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to rest with his wife and children."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The *Shī* says,
'Model yourself on your wife,
extend it to your brothers,
and so govern your family and state.'
Wife and children are difficult,
how can wife and children be ceased!"
"Then Sì wishes to rest with friends."
Confucius said:
"The *Shī* (*Book of Poetry*) says:
'Friends are there to help each other,
Help each other with dignified manners.'
Being a friend is difficult,
How can one rest from being a friend!"
"Then, Cì wishes to rest from farming."
Confucius said:
"The *Shī* (*Book of Poetry*) says:
'In the day you gather thatch,
At night you twist rope,
Hasten to roof the house,
Then begin to sow all the grains.'
Farming is difficult,
How can one rest from farming!"
"Then, is there nothing from which Cì can rest?"
Confucius said:
"Look at the grave;
It is a mound,
It is filled,
It is separated;
Then you will know where to rest."
Zǐgòng said:
"Great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
The common man finds respite there."
*Lièzǐ · Tiānruì* Zǐgòng was weary of learning
and said to Zhòngní:
“I wish to have rest.”
Zhòng Ní said:
“In life, there is no rest.”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Then does Cì have no place to rest?”
Zhòng Ní said:
“There is a place!
Look at his tomb,
broad like this,
enclosed like this,
mounded like this,
separated like this,
then you know where to rest.”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
the small man is buried there.”
Zhòng Ní said:
“Cì,
you understand it.
People all know the joy of life,
but do not know the bitterness of life;
know the weariness of old age,
but do not know the ease of old age;
know the evil of death,
but do not know the rest of death.”
*Dà Dài Lǐ · Quàn Xué* Confucius said:
"I once spent the whole day thinking,
It's better to study for even a short while;
I have tried standing on tiptoe to look at it,
It's not as good as climbing high to see broadly.
Climbing high and waving,
It's not that one's arm is long,
Yet what is seen is far away;
Shouting with the wind,
It's not that the voice is louder,
Yet what is heard is distinct.
One who uses carriages and horses,
It's not that their feet are swift,
Yet they reach a thousand *lǐ*;
One who uses boats and oars,
It's not that they are good at swimming,
Yet they cross rivers and seas.
The nature of the *jūnzǐ*,
Is not different,
But they are good at making use of things."
*Xúnzǐ*, *Yòuzuò* Confucius said:
"I have things I am ashamed of,
I have things I despise,
I have things I worry about.
When young, not being able to strive to learn,
When old, having nothing to teach,
I am ashamed of this;
Leaving one's hometown,
Serving a ruler and becoming successful,
Eventually encountering an old friend,
"If someone has no regard for the sayings of the past,
I despise him.
If someone associates with petty people,
I am wary of him."
*Xúnzǐ · Yòuzuò* Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one advances like an ant hill,
I will support him.
If one stops like a hill,
I will cease my support."
Nowadays, learning has not even reached the level of a wart or wen,
yet people presumptuously desire to be teachers.
*Xúnzǐ · Yòuzuò* Zǐgòng observed the northern hall of the Lǔ temple,
came out, and asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Just now,
I, Cì, observed the northern hall of the Grand Temple.
I did not stop looking,
and kept repeatedly gazing at the nine canopies, all of which were joined together.
Is there an explanation for this?
Did the craftsmen overdo it?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The hall of the Grand Temple once had an explanation.
Officials hired skilled craftsmen,
who added beautiful details and ornamentation.
It's not that there was a lack of good materials,
but rather, the emphasis was on refined decoration."
*Xúnzǐ · Zǐdào* Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ,
"Does a *jūnzǐ* also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The superior man,
when he has not yet attained something,
delights in the intention of it;
once he has attained it,
he delights in its management.
Therefore, he has lifelong joy,
without a single day of sorrow.
The petty man,
when he has not yet attained something,
worries about not attaining it;
once he has attained it,
he fears losing it.
Therefore, he has lifelong sorrow,
without a single day of joy."
*Shuō Yuàn · Zá Yán* Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Does the superior man also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
The superior man cultivates his conduct;
before attaining something,
he delights in the intention of it;
once he has attained it,
he delights in understanding it.
Therefore, he has lifelong joy,
without a single day of sorrow.
The petty man is not like this;
before attaining something,
he worries about not attaining it;
Having already obtained it,
one then fears losing it.
Therefore, one has worries all day long,
without a single day of joy."
*Xúnzǐ, Fǎ Xíng* Kǒngzǐ said:
"The junzi has three considerations
that one cannot but consider:
If young and not learning,
when grown, one will be incapable.
If old and not teaching,
upon death, one will not be remembered.
If possessing and not giving,
when impoverished, one will have no helpers.
Therefore, the junzi, when young, considers being grown and then learns;
when old, considers death and then teaches;
when possessing, considers poverty and then gives."
*Yù Lǎn* 607 quotes *Shènzǐ* Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiū was fond of learning when young
and heard the Dao later in life.
This is how I became broad in knowledge."
*Qúnshū Zhìyào,* *Shīzǐ · Quàn Xué* Fūzǐ said:
"For a carriage,
one only fears the ground not being solid; for a boat,
one only fears the water not being deep.
If one possesses the tools,
then one can turn what is difficult for people into what is easy.
Now the Dao
turns what is difficult for people into what is easy."
*Qún Shū Zhì Yào*, *Shī Zǐ*·*Chǔ Dào*: Confucius said:
"If you wish to know, then ask;
if you wish to be capable, then learn;
if you wish to be sufficient, then prepare beforehand;
if you wish to be good, then practice diligently.
If the state is in turmoil, then select the wicked people and remove them,
then the state will be governed well;
if one's heart is in turmoil,
then select the wicked desires and cast them away,
then virtue will be rectified."
*Yì Lín* quotes *Shī Zǐ*: Confucius said:
"Reciting poetry and reading books is
to dwell with the ancients;
reading books and reciting poetry is
to deliberate with the ancients."
*Zhuāng Zǐ*·*Zá Piān*·*Ràng Wáng*: Confucius said to Yán Huí:
"Huí! Come here.
Your family is poor and your dwelling is humble,
why don't you take office?"
Yán Huí replied:
"I do not wish to take office.
Huí has fifty *mǔ* of fields outside the city,
enough to provide thin gruel;
ten *mǔ* of fields inside the city,
enough to provide silk and hemp;
playing the zither
is enough to amuse myself;
what I have learned from the Master's Way
enough to bring joy to oneself.
Huí does not wish to serve."
Kǒngzǐ changed his expression gravely and said:
"Excellent!
The intention of Huí.
I have heard it said,
those who know contentment
are not burdened by profit;
those who carefully understand what they have gained for themselves
do not fear losing it;
those who cultivate themselves internally
are not ashamed even without a position.
I have recited this for a long time,
and now I see it exemplified in Huí,
this is my gain."
*Lǚshì Chūnqiū · Jìchūn Jì · Zūn Shī* Zigòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"How will later generations refer to you, Master?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How can I be worthy of praise?
If I must say something,
it would be that I love learning and am never tired of it,
I love teaching and am never weary,
is it perhaps only this?"
*Huáinánzǐ · Yàolüè* Kǒngzǐ cultivated the Way of Chéng and Kāng,
and transmitted the teachings of the Duke of Zhōu,
to teach his seventy disciples.
He made them wear the appropriate clothing,
and study the writings,
Therefore, this is how Confucian scholars should study.
*Shuō Yuàn · Jiàn Běn*: Confucius said to Zǐlù:
"What do you like?"
Zǐlù said:
"I like long swords."
Confucius said:
"That is not what I am asking.
If you take what you are already capable of,
and add learning to it,
how far could you go!"
Zǐlù said:
"Is learning also beneficial?"
Confucius said:
"If a ruler has no ministers to remonstrate with him, he will err in government;
if a scholar has no teaching friends, he will lose virtue.
One does not release the whip from a wild horse,
nor does one remove the bow from the bow-straightening frame.
Wood straightened with a string becomes straight,
a person who accepts advice becomes wise.
Accepting learning and valuing inquiry,
who would not smoothly succeed?
To destroy benevolence and despise scholars
is close to inviting punishment.
A gentleman cannot do without learning."
Zǐlù said:
"There is bamboo on Nánshān [Southern Mountain]
that is straight without being bent;
when cut and used for shooting arrows,
penetrating rhinoceros hide.
What further learning is needed?"

and trustworthiness makes people rely on you.
If a person is loved,
if a person gives,
if a person is relied upon,
then he will surely avoid calamity.
He can govern a state,
how much more so himself!"

took leave of Zhòng Ní. He said:
"Shall I give you a carriage?

Zǐ Lù said:
"Please give me words."
Zhòng Ní said:
"Without strength, one cannot go far;
without toil, there is no achievement;
without loyalty, there are no relatives;
without trustworthiness, there is no return;
without respect, there is no propriety.
Be careful of these five,
and you can last for a long time."

with excess, they become extravagant;

indulging desires leads to ruin.
Have measure in food and drink,
"Clothing should have its limits;
palaces should have their standards;
possessions should have their numbers;

understands the principles of emotions and nature,
is versed in the changes of things,
knows the reasons for the hidden and the manifest,

then one can be called an accomplished person.
Having understood the Way of Heaven,
one conducts oneself with benevolence and righteousness,
Cultivate oneself with propriety and music.

are the practices of a complete person.

Kǒngzǐ said:

Kǒngzǐ said:

Zhòngní
was a person from Lǔ.
When he was born, he did not know the origin of the Yì (Changes).
I once divined his fate,
and obtained the hexagram *Lǚ* (旅, The Wanderer).
I sought further explanation from Shāng Qú shì. He said,
"You possess the wisdom of a sage but lack a position."
Kǒngzǐ wept and said,
"It is Heaven! It is fate!
The phoenix does not appear,
and the Yellow River produces no chart.
Alas!
It is the decree of Heaven!"
After finishing this lament, he ceased his ambition,
stopped reading the *Lǐ* (禮, Rites),
and halted his historical editing.
At fifty, he mastered the *Yì* (易, Book of Changes),
and wrote the *Shí Yì* (十翼, Ten Wings),
clarifying it,
clarifying the subtle teachings of the *Yì*.
He said:
"Working all day long,
I contemplate the ancient sages,
and take Yí (頤, Nourishment) as my teacher, and follow the laws of Jī Chāng and Fǎ Dàn."
He wrote *Jiǔ Wèn* (九問, Nine Questions), *Shí È* (十惡, Ten Evils),

the Upper and Lower Appended Statements,
the Great Way, the Great Numbers,
the Great Laws, and the Great Meanings.
Within the *Yì* book is a question for communicating with the sacred;
the enlightened consider it to be the work of sages and worthies.
Confucius said:
"I observe them and say that,
the benevolent see it as the pattern of benevolence, the subtleties of benevolence,
the wise see it as the questions of wisdom, the subtleties of wisdom,
and the sage sees it as the pattern of communication with the divine.
The benevolent see it and practice benevolence,
the wise see it and practice wisdom.
They follow benevolence and wisdom."
*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù*. Confucius said:
"The *Yì* is,
ease,
change,
and constancy.
It governs the three achievements and virtues,
and embraces the subtle and profound aspects of the Way.
The *Yì*
speaks of its virtue,
communicates feelings without a gate,
and conceals spirit without an interior.
Its brightness pervades in all four directions,
and through interaction, principles are established.
Heaven and Earth shine brightly,
the sun, moon, and stars are arranged,
the eight trigrams are placed in their order,
the musical scales and calendar are harmonized,
the five planets follow their orbits,
and the four seasons bring harmonious budding and fruition.
The four rivers communicate feelings,
Leisurely and trustworthy in purity,
rooted amidst the floating stream,
the vital energy further substantiates each other,
emptiness evokes emotion,
purity and stillness illuminate wisdom,
moving objects to bring forth brilliance,
utmost sincerity, focused and secret,
not vexed, not yielding,
detached, yet not lost.
This is its ease.
Changeability is,
its vital energy.
Heaven and earth, if unchanging,
cannot circulate their energies.
The Five Elements alternately end and begin,
the Four Seasons replace and abolish each other.
Ruler and ministers take their images,
changing their deportment to harmonize with each other,
those who can dissipate will rest,
those who are necessarily single-minded will fail.
Ruler and ministers, if unchanging,
cannot form a dynasty.
Zhòu acted with cruelty,
heaven and earth rebelled.
King Wén employed Lǚ,
and a nine-tailed fox was seen.
Husband and wife, if unchanging,
cannot form a family.
Dájǐ indulged in favoritism,
and Yīn was destroyed because of it.
Dà Rèn followed the proper seasons,
and the dynasty enjoyed the country for seven hundred years.
This is the aspect of change.
What is unchanging
is its position.
Heaven is above,
earth is below,
the ruler faces south,
the ministers face north,
the father sits, the son prostrates.
This is the aspect of what does not change.
Therefore, change is
the way of Heaven and Earth.
The virtue of Qián and Kūn
is the treasure of all things.
How supreme is the *Yì*,
using unity as the basis for all principles."
Confucius said:
"In the time of remote antiquity,
the people were undifferentiated,
all things were indistinguishable,
and there were no benefits from clothing, food, or utensils.
Thereupon, Fúxī looked up to observe the images in the heavens,
looked down to observe the patterns on the earth,
and observed the suitability of all things in between.
He then created the eight trigrams,
To communicate the virtues of the spirits,
and to categorize the emotions of all things.
Therefore, the *Yì* [Book of Changes]
is that by which Heaven and Earth are continued,
the principles of human relationships are ordered, and the Way of the King is clarified.
Therefore, the eight trigrams are established,
the five *qì* are set in place,
and the five constant virtues are enacted by them.
It imitates the patterns of *Qián* (Heaven) and *Kūn* (Earth),
accords with *yīn* and *yáng*,
to rectify the righteousness of ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife.
It measures the times and regulates what is appropriate,
and makes nets and snares
for hunting and fishing,
to provide for the people's needs.
Thereupon, the people are well-governed,
the ruler and parents are honored,
ministers and sons are obedient,
all living beings live in harmony,
and each finds peace in its own nature.
This is the use of the eight trigrams.
When *Fúxī* shì ruled the world,
he first created the eight trigrams,
and knotted cords to make nets and snares,
for hunting and fishing.
This was taken from the *Lí* trigram.
The substance is without embellishment;
speaking with respect to Heaven,
This is the meaning of change in the *Yì*.
The transformations of the eight trigrams
are images that resonate with people.
Wén Wáng, according to the suitability of human nature and emotions,
created regulations for them."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Yì* begins with the Supreme Ultimate (*Tàijí*).
The Supreme Ultimate divides and becomes two,
thus giving birth to Heaven and Earth.
Heaven and Earth have the seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
thus giving birth to the four seasons.
Each of the four seasons has divisions of yin and yang, firmness and gentleness,
thus giving birth to the eight trigrams.
When the eight trigrams are arranged,
the Way of Heaven and Earth is established,
and the images of thunder, wind, water, fire, mountain, and marsh are determined.
Their distribution and application in affairs is such that
*zhèn* generates things in the east,
its position is in the second month;
*xùn* scatters them in the southeast,
its position is in the fourth month;
*lí* causes them to grow in the south,
its position is in the fifth month;
*kūn* nourishes them in the southwest,
its position is in the sixth month;
*duì* gathers them in the west,
its position is in the eighth month;
*qián* controls them in the northwest,
Lí is located in the tenth month;
Kǎn is hidden in the north,
located in the eleventh month;
Gèn finishes and begins in the northeast,
located in the twelfth month.
When the qi of the eight trigrams ends,
then the distinctions of the four cardinal directions and four corners are clear,
the ways of birth, growth, gathering, and storage are complete,
the substance of yin and yang is settled,
the virtue of spiritual enlightenment is communicated,
and the myriad things are each completed according to their kind.
All are encompassed by the *Yì*.
How perfect!
The virtue of the *Yì*."
*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù*. Kǒngzǐ said:
"The year has three hundred and sixty days, and the heavenly qi cycles completely.
The eight trigrams each govern for forty-five days,
thus completing the year.
Therefore, Gèn gradually advances in the first month,
Xùn gradually advances in the third month,
Kūn gradually advances in the seventh month,
Qián gradually advances in the ninth month,
and each month is according to what is said in the trigram.
Qián is
Heaven,
ending and becoming the beginning of all things;
the north
is where all things begin,
Therefore, the position of Qián is in the tenth month.
Gèn means,
that which stops things.
Therefore, it is at the end of the four seasons,
its position is in the twelfth month;
Xùn means,
the Yin begins to follow the Yang,
the Yang begins to grow strong in the southeast,
therefore its position is in the fourth month.
Kūn means,
the way of the Earth,
its form is established in the sixth month,
the four cardinal directions are correctly ordered,
the warp and weft are balanced,
and the sequence of degrees is complete."
Confucius said:
"Qián and Kūn are,
the masters of Yin and Yang.
Yang begins in Hài,
takes shape in Chǒu,
the position of Qián is in the northwest,
Yang's ancestor subtly relies on the beginning.
Yin begins in Sì,
takes shape in Wèi,
relying on correctness to establish its position,
therefore the position of Kūn is in the southwest,
the correctness of Yin.
The way of the ruler initiates,
The way of a minister is ultimately to be upright,
therefore the position of Qián 乾 is in hài 亥,
and the position of Kūn 坤 is in wèi 未.
This is to clarify the duties of yin and yang
and establish the positions of ruler and minister."
Confucius said:
"Once the order of the eight trigrams is established,
then the five elements transform into shapes.
Therefore, when a person is born, they correspond to the structure of the eight trigrams,
and receive the five elements to become the five constant virtues,
which are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness.
All things initially emerge from Zhèn 震, Zhèn,
is the trigram of the east.
The yang qi begins to generate,
receiving the way of form,
therefore the east is associated with benevolence.
They are completed in Lí 離, Lí,
is the trigram of the south.
Yang obtains its proper position above,
yin obtains its proper position below,
the image of superior and inferior is established,
which is the order of propriety,
therefore the south is associated with propriety.
They enter into Duì 兌, Duì,
is the trigram of the west.
Yin takes charge and all things obtain what is suitable,
which is the principle of righteousness,
therefore the west is associated with righteousness.
Gradually [becoming] like Kan; Kan,
is the hexagram of the north,
the yin energy is strong in form,
the yin and yang energies are contained and closed,
[it is] the category of trustworthiness,
therefore the north is trustworthiness.
Now, the meanings of the four directions
are all governed by the center,
therefore Qian, Kun, Gen, Xun,
are located in the four corners,
the center is that by which the four directions are governed,
[it is] the decision of wisdom,
therefore the center is wisdom.
Therefore the Way arises from benevolence,
is established in ritual,
is ordered by righteousness,
is settled in trustworthiness,
is completed in wisdom.
These five,
are the divisions of morality,
and the boundary between heaven and man.
The sages therefore understand the will of heaven,
regulate human relationships, and illuminate the ultimate Way."

Xián and Héng
are the beginning of male and female,
the way of husband and wife.
The flourishing of humanity
must come from husband and wife,
therefore they serve the ancestors,
and become masters of Heaven and Earth.

is to value them.

Confucius said:

nurturing the myriad things;
*Fǒu* is when

*yīn* and *yáng* are not in action,
and the growth of the myriad things stops.

therefore *Qián* is taken as the beginning,
and *Kūn* as the next,
first *Tài* and then *Fǒu*.
*Sǔn* is when *yīn* is in action,
the marsh diminishes the mountain, and the myriad things diminish,
the lower diminish to serve the upper;
*Yì* is when *yáng* is in action,
and thunder and wind benefit the myriad things,
the upper diminish themselves to benefit the lower.
The Lower Canon takes Yin as its model,
therefore it begins with Xián (咸),
and follows with Héng (恒).
First decrease and then increase,
each following its kind."

is the hexagram of the twelfth month.
The Yang Qi rises upward,
the Yin Qi desires to receive it,
and all things begin to advance.
It is like King Wén's (文王) cultivation of accumulated virtue,
and the grand opening of his foundation,
beginning on the path of great peace.
At this time,
neighboring states are transformed,
and the people of Qí (岐) are harmonious and well-disposed.
Therefore, the sixth in the fourth place receives favor and inherits good fortune,
and the ninth in the third place can occupy the royal position,
and make offerings at Mount Qí (岐山),
as a way of repaying virtue.
Manifesting Yin to reveal the transformation of Yang,
the people and ministers follow virtue,
therefore it is said that there is no blame."
*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù* Confucius said:

perhaps bestows it with ten pairs of tortoise shells,
and cannot be opposed.
*Yǒng zhēn jí*,
*wáng yòng xiǎng yú dì*. *Jí*,
the *yì* (increase)
is the hexagram of the first month.

all things benefit.

implementing governance and teachings,
and the world being covered by the virtue of *yáng*,
receiving the king's transformative influence,
like beautiful treasure,

"The king uses sacrifice to the Emperor"

The suburban sacrifices of the Three Kings
all used the Xia calendar.
The heavenly energy accumulates in small increments to form a manifestation;

Heaven and Earth interact,
all things communicate.

are all based on the Xia calendar.

an unchanging Way.
Therefore, the suburban sacrifices of the Three Kings
all used the Xia calendar,
in order to accord with the four seasons

*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù* (Apochryphal Commentary on the Book of Changes) Confucius said:
"In the *Suí* hexagram, line six at the top,
is restrained and bound,
and then follows from the rope.
The king uses it to make offerings on Mount Xī.
*Suí* is the hexagram of the second month.
The virtue of *Suí* is put into practice,
[when] the fence is broken and difficult to untie,
all things follow the yang and emerge.
Therefore, line six at the top desires that nine in the fifth place restrain and bind it,
and maintain it,
illustrating being influenced by the transformation of yang, and the yin following and complying.
It is like King Wén's exaltation of supreme virtue,
manifesting the beauty of equilibrium and harmony,
restraining the people with ritual,
and binding the people with righteousness.
At this time,
where benevolence and grace are bestowed,
none do not follow and comply.
All delight in his virtue,
and obtain a king who employs the Way.
Therefore, it is said that the king uses it to make offerings on Mount Xī."
Confucius said:
"When *yáng* diminishes, *yīn* speaks.
When *yīn* diminishes, *yáng* speaks of stripping away.
This is the origin of all things.
To sever, control, eliminate harm,
and make the preservation of things one's task
is what is meant by *jué* (決, Resoluteness).
When it is the time of the third month,
*yáng* is flourishing and growing, *yīn* dwindling and ceasing,
and the *qì* of *yīn*
all things are completely born,
without exception, receiving transformation.
It is like a king who exalts supreme virtue,
reverently receiving Heaven's mandate,
decisively eliminating petty people,
in order to bring peace to the common people;
therefore it is called *jué*.
The harm done by *yīn* becomes an action;
therefore, to strip away becomes the action of stripping.
When it is the time of the ninth month,
the *yáng qì* declines and diminishes,
but *yīn* ultimately cannot completely overcome *yáng*;
petty people cannot decisively eliminate gentlemen.
This is called *bō* (剝, Stripping Away),
meaning unease and nothing more.
Therefore, regarding the ninth and fifth lines, it speaks of *jué*;
petty people strip it away.
Regarding the sixth and fifth lines, it speaks of flourishing and killing all things;
all strip off and fall away.
It is like the way of the superior man declining,
and the way of the petty man flourishing,
aggressive actions arising,
and the way of safety being abandoned.
The *yīn* line pierces through like a string of fish, wanting to receive the superior man."
*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù*. Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Yì* has six positions and three powers,
which are the boundaries of the ways of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
The ways of the three powers
are Heaven, Earth, and Man.
Heaven has *yīn* and *yáng*,
Earth has yielding and firm,
Man has benevolence and righteousness.
Emulating these three,
therefore the six positions are produced.
The changes of the six positions:
the *yáng* lines
are governed by Heaven,
the *yīn* lines
are connected to Earth.
Heaven moves and bestows, which is called benevolence;
Earth is still and manages, which is called righteousness.
When benevolence is completed, it rises upwards;
when righteousness is completed, it descends downwards.
That which is above solely governs,
that which is below obediently follows.
When correctness takes form in man,
then moral principles are established and hierarchy is determined.
This is the dividing line between the Way of Heaven and Earth and the Way of Man.
The Qi of Heaven and Earth
must have a beginning and an end.
The arrangement of the six positions
all follows the order of above and below.
Therefore, the *Yì* begins with One,
divides into Two,
connects into Three,
*[illegible]* into Four,
flourishes into Five,
and ends with Above.
The initial position is *yuán shì* (元士, primary scholar),
the second is *dàfū* (大夫, grand master),
the third is *sāngōng* (三公, the three dukes/ministers),
the fourth is *zhūhóu* (諸侯, feudal lords),
the fifth is *tiānzǐ* (天子, the Son of Heaven),
and the upper position is the ancestral temple (*zōngmiào* 宗廟).
All these six are
how Yin and Yang advance and retreat,
how ruler and subject ascend and descend,
and how the myriad people take them as models.
Therefore, Yin and Yang have waxing and waning,
and the Way of Man has gain and loss.
The sage observes these phenomena,
follows their changes,
and establishes hexagrams accordingly.
When something is flourishing, it presages good fortune;
when it is about to decline, it foreshadows misfortune.
If Yin and Yang are not correct,
it is all due to a loss of position,
and when the response is substantial and possessed,
it is all a loss of righteousness.
Even if goodness is slight,
it will inevitably show auspicious signs;
Even if evil is minute,
there will certainly be regret and distress.
Therefore, to fully understand the changes of heaven and earth,
and to exhaust the true nature of all things,
is the task of an enlightened ruler.
Qiū explained it, saying:
"Establish images to fully express meaning,
set up the guà to fully express true and false intentions,
attach explanations to them to fully express their words."
*Zhōu Yì Qián Záo Dù* Confucius said:
"When the six positions of the *Yì* are correct,
the standards of the ruler will be revealed."

Dàjūn is

A dà rén is one whose
sage-like intelligence and virtuous character are complete.

and inscribe virtue to distinguish conduct.
A wáng is

King Zhāo of Chǔ fell ill,
and divined about it, saying:

The king said:

the former kings divided the land and established territories,

*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*, Seven. Confucius said:
"Enlightened rulers have three fears:
first, being in a high position and fearing that they will not hear their faults;
second, achieving their ambitions and fearing arrogance;
third, hearing the ultimate Way of the world and fearing that they will not be able to put it into practice."
*Dà Dài Lǐ · Zhǔ Yán*.
Confucius was at leisure,
and Zēng Zǐ (曾子) was attending him.
Confucius said,
"Cān (參),
the gentlemen of today are only between the words of the shì (士) and the dàfū (大夫);
those who reach the words of a true gentleman
are very rare.
Alas!
Will my words of a ruler die without being spoken?
How sad!"
Zēng Zǐ (曾子) rose and said,
"May I ask, what are the words of a ruler?"
Confucius did not answer.
Zēng Zǐ (曾子) was afraid,
respectfully adjusted his clothes, descended from his mat, and said,
"Your disciple knows his disrespect.
It is difficult to obtain the leisure of the Master,
therefore I dared to ask."
Confucius did not answer.
Zēng Zǐ was apprehensive.
He stepped back, leaned against the west wall, and stood there.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shēn,
can you discuss the Way of an enlightened ruler?"
Zēng Zǐ said:
"I dare not consider myself sufficient.
It is difficult to receive leisure time from you, Master,
therefore I dare to ask."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I will tell you.
The Way
is that by which virtue is illuminated;
virtue
is that by which the Way is honored.
Therefore, without virtue there is no honor,
without the Way there is no illumination.
Though one has state horses,
if they are not taught, they will not be obedient,
and one cannot travel a thousand *lǐ*.
Though one has broad lands and many people,
if one does not govern the land properly,
one cannot become a hegemonic ruler.
Therefore, the enlightened rulers of old
cultivated internally the Seven Teachings,
and practiced externally the Three Attainments.
If the Seven Teachings are cultivated, one can defend;
if the Three Attainments are practiced, one can conquer.
If the seven teachings are not cultivated,
even if one defends, it will not be secure;
if the three visits are not carried out,
even if one attacks, they will not submit.
Therefore, the defense of a wise ruler
must be to deter aggression a thousand *lǐ* away;
and their attack
is to return the army from the mat and seat.
Therefore, cultivate the seven teachings internally and the ruler will not be burdened;
carry out the three visits externally and wealth will not be wasted.
This is called the way of a wise ruler."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I ask whether it is possible to be considered wise without wasting or being burdened?"
Kǒngzǐ became stern and raised his eyebrows, saying:
"Shēn,
do you consider a wise ruler to be burdened?
In the past, Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāoyáo on his right,
and without leaving his seat, the world was governed.
If the administration is not correct,
it is the fault of the ruler;
if the administration is correct,
but orders are not carried out,
it is the fault of those in charge of their duties.
Why would a wise ruler be burdened?
In the past, wise rulers inspected the borders without levying taxes,
visited markets without collecting duties,
taxed at a rate of one-tenth,
To employ the strength of the people,
[it] should not exceed three days per year;
entering the mountains and marshes should be done according to the seasons,
with prohibitions but without levies.
These six things
are ways to acquire wealth.
An enlightened ruler abandons four of these and moderates the other two;
how then does an enlightened ruler obtain his expenses?"
Zēng Zǐ said:
"May I venture to ask what are the Seven Instructions?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"If those above respect the elderly, then those below will become more filial;
if those above follow seniority, then those below will become more fraternal;
if those above enjoy giving, then those below will become more trustworthy;
if those above are close to the virtuous, then those below will choose their friends carefully;
if those above love virtue, then those below will not conceal [their faults];
if those above hate greed, then those below will be ashamed to contend;
if those above are steadfast and resolute, then those below will value integrity and honor;
when the people all have distinctions [of rank and duty],
then [they will be] upright and correct.
[This] is also not laborious.
This is called the Seven Instructions.
The Seven Instructions
are the foundation for governing the people;
when the instructions are settled, then things are rectified.
Those above
are the models for the people;
if the models are correct, then what thing will not be correct?
Therefore, if the ruler first establishes himself in benevolence,
then the senior officials will be loyal and the scholars trustworthy,
the common people will be honest,
the artisans simple,
the merchants sincere,
the young women innocent,
and the married women unassuming.
These seven
are the aims of education.
When these seven are spread throughout the world, they will not be excessive;
when confined to ordinary rooms, they will not be obstructed.
Therefore, the sage equalizes them with ritual,
establishes them with righteousness,
and carries them out with obedience,
and the people will cast off evil as if by washing."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Your disciple is not up to it,
but the principle is perfect."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shēn,
let us stop there;
there is more.
In the past, enlightened rulers had methods for governing the people;
they necessarily divided the land into provinces,
assigning them to different jurisdictions for governance.
In this way, virtuous people had nowhere to hide,
and violent people had nowhere to conceal themselves.
They made officials examine the people daily,
If you examine them regularly,
and yearly encourage the virtuous,
then the virtuous will become close,
and the unworthy will be fearful.
Cause them to care for widowers and widows,
care for orphans and the solitary,
relieve the poor and impoverished,
encourage filial piety and brotherly respect,
and select the wise and promote the able.
If these seven things are cultivated,
then within the four seas,
there will be no people subject to punishment.
If those above treat those below as intimately as their own heart and belly,
then those below will treat those above as fondly as a child seeing its loving mother.
When those above and those below are so close to each other,
then orders will be followed,
and policies will be implemented.
Because the people who are already near are pleased,
those who are far away will come and submit.
Then, by spreading your fingers you will know an inch,
by spreading your hand you will know a foot,
by extending your elbow you will know a fathom,
ten fathoms make a cable's length.
One hundred paces make a wall,
three hundred paces make a *lǐ*,
one thousand paces make a well,
three wells make a *gōuliè*,
three *gōuliè* make a *jù*,
If fiefs are established every fifty *lǐ*,
and cities are established every hundred *lǐ*,
then provisions of clothing and furs will be stored.
This makes those who reside secure,
and those who travel have [a sense of] rise and fall [security when travelling].
Therefore, the *Mányí* barbarians and the various *Xià* peoples,
though their clothing and language are different,
none fail to come
to have an audience with the king.
Therefore it is said:
Even without markets, the people will not lack;
even without punishments, the people will not disobey.
The gains from netting birds, hunting, and tilling
are not used to fill the palaces;
what is collected from the people
is not used to fill the storehouses.
Extravagance is curbed to compensate for what is insufficient,
and rituals are used to reduce what is superfluous.
Therefore it is said:
With much sincerity and little outward appearance,
its rites can be preserved,
its trustworthiness can be relied upon,
and its traces can be followed.
Its trustworthiness
is like the four seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
its embrace of the myriad people
is like eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty.
The people of the lower lands trust in this!
The heat of summer and the cold of winter,
though far away, are brought near.
It is not that the Way is near,
but that its shining virtue extends.
Therefore, without moving armies, one inspires awe;
without dispensing benefits, one gains affection.
This is what is meant by the vigilance of an enlightened ruler.
"To parry attacks a thousand *lǐ* away,
this is what it refers to."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask what are the Three Perfections (sān zhì)?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Perfect propriety needs no yielding, yet the world is well-governed;
perfect rewards need no expenditure, yet the scholars of the world are pleased;
perfect music is without sound, yet the people of the world are in harmony.
An enlightened ruler earnestly practices the Three Perfections;
therefore, the rulers of the world can be known,
the scholars of the world can be made his ministers,
and the people of the world can be employed."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask what they are?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In ancient times, enlightened rulers exhausted their knowledge of the names of the world's worthy scholars.
Having known their names,
they also knew their numbers;
having known their numbers,
they also knew their locations.
Enlightened rulers used the ranks of the world to honor the scholars of the world;
This is called the ultimate propriety: not yielding, yet the world is governed.
Distributing the wealth of the world,
to enrich the scholars of the world,
this is called the ultimate reward: not wasteful, yet the scholars of the world are pleased.
When the scholars of the world are pleased,
then the brilliant reputation of the world will flourish;
this is called the ultimate joy: without sound, yet the people of the world are harmonious.
Therefore it is said:
the so-called ultimate benevolence in the world
is the ability to unite those who are most closely related in the world;
the so-called ultimate wisdom in the world
is the ability to employ those who are most harmonious in the world;
the so-called ultimate discernment in the world
is the ability to select those who are most virtuous in the world.
When these three are all interconnected,
then one can undertake a campaign.
Therefore, for the benevolent, there is nothing greater than loving others;
for the wise, there is nothing greater than knowing the worthy;
for the ruler, there is nothing greater than employing the worthy.
If the ruler of a state cultivates these three,
then all within the four seas will respectfully watch,
and then he can undertake a campaign.
What an enlightened ruler attacks
must be where the Way is abandoned.
If they abandon the Way and do not practice it,
then punish their ruler,
carry out the campaign,
comfort their people, and do not seize their wealth.
Therefore, it is said:
The expeditions of an enlightened ruler
are like timely rain,
arriving to the joy of the people.
Therefore, his bestowals are exceedingly widespread,
and he gains the affection of exceedingly many.
This is what is meant by “returning with the army from upon the mat and seat."」
*Da Dai Li - Wu Di De* Zǎi Wǒ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"In the past, I heard from Róng Yīlìng
that the Huángdì reigned for three hundred years.
May I ask, was the Huángdì a human,
or not a human?
How did he reach three hundred years?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yǔ,
Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Chéng Wáng, Zhōu Gōng—
can they be observed exhaustively?
As for the Huángdì, he is too remote.
What do you take him to be?
The masters of old rarely spoke of him."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"The transmissions of ancient times,
obscure and subtle sayings,
fully debated distinctions,
and careless intentions,
are not the way of a gentleman.
Therefore, my question is certainly well-founded."
Kǒngzǐ said:
The Yellow Emperor,
was the son of Shǎo Diǎn,
named Xuān Yuán.
He was born with a divine spirit,
able to speak when young,
intelligent from childhood,
earnest and quick-witted when grown,
and discerning upon adulthood.
He governed the five qì,
established the five measures,
comforted the myriad people,
measured the four directions,
and taught the bears, *bā*, *pí*, leopards, and tigers,
to fight the Red Emperor in the wilderness of Bǎn Quán.
After three battles,
he was then able to achieve his ambition.
The Yellow Emperor wore an embroidered coat and skirt,
a large belt,
and an embroidered skirt,
riding a dragon and leaning on a cloud-patterned screen,
to conform to the principles of Heaven and Earth,
the reasons for darkness and light,
the explanations of life and death,
and the difficulties of survival and destruction.
He sowed the various grains, grasses, and trees in season,
therefore, his teachings transformed birds, beasts, insects, and other creatures,
observed the movements of the sun, moon, and stars,
and thoroughly exploited the earth, stones, metals, and jades.
Exerting his mind, strength, ears, and eyes,
He conserved water, fire, materials, and resources.
While alive, the people benefited from him for a hundred years;
After his death, the people feared his spirit for a hundred years;
After his passing, the people applied his teachings for a hundred years.
Therefore, it is said, "three hundred years."
Zǎi Wǒ asked about Emperor Zhuānxū.
Confucius said:
"The Five Emperors relied on explanations,
The Three Kings relied on measurements and standards.
You want to understand and distinguish the sayings of the ancient past in one day?
How rash you are, Yǔ!"
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"In the past, I heard from you, Master, that:
'The young ones should have no lingering questions.'"
Confucius said:
"Zhuānxū
was the grandson of the Yellow Emperor,
and the son of Chāngyì;
He was called Gāoyáng.
With deep and profound wisdom, he possessed strategies;
He was clear and thorough, and understood matters;
He nurtured resources to suit the land;
He followed the seasons to emulate Heaven;
He relied on ghosts and spirits to establish righteousness;
He regulated the Qi to instruct the people;
He used purity and sincerity in sacrifices.
Riding dragons, he reached the four seas,
Reaching north to Yōulíng,
south to Jiāozhǐ,
west crossing the moving sands,
and east to Pánmù.
Moving and still things,
great and small spirits,
all that the sun and moon illuminate,
none fail to be reverent and diligent."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Dì Kù?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He was the grandson of Yuán Xiāo,
the son of Tǎn Jí,
named Gāo Xīn.
Born divine and spiritual,
he named himself.
He generously bestowed benefits on all things,
not for his own sake.
With his intelligence, he knew what was distant;
with his clarity, he observed what was subtle.
He followed the righteousness of Heaven
and understood the people's needs.
He was benevolent yet authoritative,
kind yet trustworthy.
He cultivated himself, and the world submitted.
He took the wealth of the land but used it sparingly.
He nurtured and taught the myriad people and profited them with instruction.
He calculated the days and months to welcome and send them off.
He clarified the spirits and gods and respectfully served them.
His countenance was dignified,
his virtue lofty.
His actions were timely,
his attire befitting a scholar.
In spring and summer, he rode dragons;
in autumn and winter, he rode horses.
He wore yellow fǔ and fú robes,
maintained the middle way, and thus gained the empire.
Wherever the sun and moon shone,
wherever wind and rain reached,
none failed to follow and obey him."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Dì Yáo?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He was the son of Gāo Xīn,
named Fàng Xūn.
His benevolence was like Heaven,
his wisdom like the spirits.
Approaching him was like approaching the sun,
beholding him was like beholding the clouds.
He was wealthy but not arrogant,
noble but not haughty.
He wore yellow fǔ and fú robes,
rode in a red carriage with white horses.
Bó Yí presided over the rites,
Lóng and Kuí taught dancing.
He promoted Shùn and Péng Zǔ and entrusted them with responsibilities.
The Xiānmín (先民, Former Sages) governed them according to the four seasons.
He exiled Gònggōng (共工) to Yōuzhōu (幽州),
in order to transform the Northern Dí (北狄, Northern Barbarians);
banished Dōu (兜) to Chóngshān (崇山),
in order to transform the Southern Mán (南蠻, Southern Barbarians);
executed Sāmiáo (三苗) at Sānwēi (三危),
in order to transform the Western Róng (西戎, Western Barbarians);
and executed Gǔn (鯀) at Yǔshān (羽山),
in order to transform the Eastern Yí (東夷, Eastern Barbarians).
His words were consistent,
his virtue did not deviate.
Within the four seas,
wherever boats and carriages reached,
none did not rejoice in his governance."
Zǎi Wǒ (宰我) said:
"May I ask about Emperor Shùn (舜)?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"He was the grandson of Jiǎo Niú (蟜牛),
the son of Gǔ Sǒu (瞽叟),
named Chóng Huá (重華).
He loved learning and was filial and fraternal,
known throughout the four seas.
As a potter, he served his parents,
with generosity, gentleness, kindness, and goodness.
He taught with sincerity and knew the times,
he feared Heaven and loved the people,
he cared for those far away and was close to his relatives.
He received the great mandate,
Relying on Ní Huáng,
wise, insightful, and understanding,
he became the king of the world.
He sent Yǔ to survey the land,
to oversee the famous mountains and rivers,
in order to benefit the people.
He sent Hòu Jì to sow seeds,
diligently cultivating fine grains,
in order to provide food and drink.
Xī Hé oversaw the calendar,
respectfully instructing the people about the seasons.
He sent Yì to manage fire,
in order to clear the mountains and scrubland.
Bó Yí was in charge of ritual,
in order to regulate the world.
Kuí created music,
to sing and dance with appeals,
harmonized with bells and drums.
Gāo Yáo was in charge of law,
loyal, trustworthy, and clear in judgment,
understanding the feelings of the people.
Qì served as Minister of Education,
teaching the people filial piety and fraternity,
respecting governance and following the classics.
His words were not deceptive,
his virtue was not concealed,
he promoted the virtuous and the world was at peace.
To the south he pacified Jiāo Zhǐ,
He greatly set free the Xiānzhī, Qúsōu, Dī, and Qiāng peoples,
as well as the Běishān, Róng, Fā, and Xīshèn peoples,
and to the east, the Cháng and Niǎoyí Yǔmín peoples.
When Shùn was young,
he suffered hardship and toil.
At twenty, he was known throughout the world for his filial piety.
At thirty, he was in position.
He succeeded to the imperial throne.
He died at fifty
and was buried in the wilds of Cāngwú."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Yǔ?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He was the grandson of Gāoyáng
and the son of Gǔn,
and was called Wénmìng.
He was quick, clever, and capable of accomplishment.
His virtue did not falter.
His benevolence was approachable.
His words were trustworthy.
His voice set the standard for musical pitch,
his person set the standard for measurement.
He was praised as the best of officials.
He was diligent and reverent,
serving as the guiding principle and organizational framework.
He toured the nine provinces,
opened up the nine roads,
managed the nine marshes,
He measured the nine mountains.
He acted as the master of the spirits,
and as the father and mother of the people.
On his left, he held the plumb line and level;
on his right, the compass and square.
He traversed the four seasons,
and governed the four seas.
He pacified the nine provinces,
and upheld the nine heavens.
He clarified sight and hearing,
and governed the world.
He promoted Gāo Yáo and Yì to assist him,
and he raised weapons to punish those unoffering, unprincipled, and immoral people.
Within the four seas,
wherever ships and carriages reached,
all submitted."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Yǔ,
his greatness is as described;
the people rejoiced to the utmost.
I am not the man for such a task."
Zǎi Wǒ said,
"I am not trustworthy enough,
but I respectfully accept the charge."
Another day,
Zǎi Wǒ told this to others.
Someone repeated this at the place where the gentlemen studied,
Kǒngzǐ said,
"If I wanted to judge people by their appearance, I
would change it because of Miè Míng (滅明);
if I wanted to judge people by their words, I
would change it because of Yǔ (予);
if I wanted to judge people by their countenance, I
would change it because of Shī (師)."
